articles.headline: Adif recepciona este miércoles la obra de la intermodal de Lugo y Conde Fontao podrá reabrir
articles.subtitle: El ente ferroviario confirmó al Concello que recibe hoy la obra completa, el trámite que faltaba para reabrir al tráfico la plaza, cortada desde finales de abril. La inauguración de la nueva estación aún no tiene fecha.
articles.body:
El Administrador de Infraestructuras Ferroviarias (Adif) recepciona este miércoles las obras de la estación intermodal de Lugo, el paso administrativo que quedaba para reabrir al tráfico la praza Conde de Fontao, cortada desde que los trabajos comenzaron a finales de abril, cuando la previsión inicial era de un mes.

El ente lo confirmó el lunes al Concello, por carta y por teléfono, en respuesta a la misiva que la alcaldesa, Elena Candia, envió el 18 de agosto al presidente de Adif para exigir un calendario tras meses de retrasos. "Ao mesmo tempo, vía telefónica, informóuselle de que está previsto que sexa o mércores cando faga ADIF a recepción da obra da empresa, que é o paso previo", explicó la regidora.

## Una recepción sin atajos

Adif descartó una recepción parcial del viario y recordó que el contrato incluye la urbanización del entorno de Conde Fontao, la rúa Alta y Sagrado Corazón. "No se podía hacer la recepción parcial de esa calle, pero una vez recepcionada la obra por Adif sí que tiene una relación directa con la apertura", insistió Candia.

La demora ha encendido la política local: el PP cargó contra el Ministerio de Transportes por "capricho político", mientras el PSOE reclamaba la "apertura inmediata ao tráfico" y acusaba al gobierno local de escudarse en el convenio. Candia respondió afeando a los socialistas su "desconocimiento" de los convenios administrativos.

La recepción no implica la puesta en servicio de la estación, que sigue sin fecha de inauguración. Una vez completado el trámite, el Concello asume la conservación y el mantenimiento del entorno remodelado, según el convenio entre Adif y el Ayuntamiento.

articles.headline: España firma en PISA 2025 sus peores resultados históricos en Lectura, Matemáticas y Ciencias
articles.subtitle: Los alumnos de 15 años evaluados con el currículo de la LOMLOE caen 23 puntos en lectura respecto a 2022 y un tercio no alcanza el nivel básico en matemáticas. El Gobierno defiende la ley; los expertos señalan a las pantallas y al modelo competencial.
articles.body:
Los alumnos españoles de 15 años han obtenido en el informe PISA 2025 sus peores resultados de la historia en Lectura, Matemáticas y Ciencias. Es la primera edición que evalúa a estudiantes formados íntegramente con el currículo de la LOMLOE, la ley educativa aprobada a finales de 2020.

España logra 451 puntos en Lectura —23 menos que en 2022 y 45 menos que en 2015—, 457 en Matemáticas y 477 en Ciencias. En las tres áreas queda por debajo de las medias de la OCDE y de la UE; en lectura, la pérdida equivale a medio curso escolar y sitúa a un quinceañero español al nivel de comprensión de un británico de 13 años.

## Un tercio por debajo de lo mínimo

El 33% de los alumnos no alcanza el nivel 2 de matemáticas, el umbral básico para desenvolverse en la vida, frente al 22% de 2015. Los de bajo rendimiento en lectura han pasado del 16% al 32% en una década.

La caída es más intensa entre los alumnos de familias acomodadas: en ciencias pierden 13 puntos desde 2022, frente a cuatro los desfavorecidos. Los expertos citan el abuso del móvil y la "tecnología del scrolling", el uso de la IA para las tareas y un currículo que, según el director de Educación de Funcas, Ismael Sanz, "lo ha apostado todo a la equidad sacrificando la calidad".

La ministra de Educación, Milagros Tolón, rechaza que la LOMLOE tenga relación con el batacazo y responsabiliza a las pantallas. La OCDE excluyó a Cataluña de las comparaciones internacionales por excluir al 23% de su muestra; el ministerio la incluyó con una nota. Galicia, con 466 puntos en matemáticas y 486 en ciencias, supera las medias de la OCDE y la UE en ambas.

articles.headline: El Supremo suspende el voto de los nacionalizados por la 'ley de nietos' salvo exilio acreditado
articles.subtitle: La Sala de lo Contencioso-Administrativo estima la medida cautelar de Vox e Iustitia Europa: los inscritos en el censo de residentes ausentes no votarán hasta la sentencia, que el tribunal quiere dictar antes de final de año. El Gobierno rechaza la decisión.
articles.body:
El Tribunal Supremo ha suspendido de forma cautelar los efectos electorales de las inscripciones en el Censo Electoral de Residentes Ausentes (CERA) de quienes obtuvieron la nacionalidad por la 'ley de nietos', y paraliza las nuevas altas, salvo que se acredite el exilio de sus antepasados mediante certificación consular.

La Sala de lo Contencioso-Administrativo estima así las medidas solicitadas por Vox y la organización Iustitia Europa, que sostienen que el Ejecutivo preparaba un "fraude masivo" en las próximas convocatorias electorales. La nacionalidad concedida no se retira: quienes ya figuran inscritos conservan su derecho de sufragio congelado hasta que el tribunal resuelva el fondo, algo que prevé "agilizar" para tener sentencia antes de final de año.

En contra se pronunciaron la Fiscalía y el Gobierno, a través de la Abogacía del Estado, que alega que la medida priva del derecho al voto a ciudadanos con nacionalidad reconocida por actos administrativos firmes. "La decisión del Supremo no la compartimos", dijo el ministro Félix Bolaños, que pidió que el asunto se resuelva "antes de los procesos electorales de 2027". Se avecina un año electoral: municipales y autonómicas en mayo y generales, como tarde, en julio.

El origen del litigio es una instrucción de Justicia de octubre de 2022 —firmada por Sofía Puente, hermana del ministro Óscar Puente— que presumía la condición de exiliado de quienes salieron de España entre el 18 de julio de 1936 y el 31 de diciembre de 1955, sin exigir documentación. Vox celebró haber "suspendido el intento de manipulación del censo electoral para alterar las elecciones"; el asunto afecta según El Mundo a hasta 2,3 millones de potenciales votantes.

articles.headline: Cataluña suspende las clases y restringe la movilidad en cinco comarcas por lluvias torrenciales
articles.subtitle: El Govern activa para este miércoles la alerta roja del plan INUNCAT en el Baix Llobregat, el Vallès Occidental, el Garraf y el Alt y Baix Penedès: sin colegios ni universidades, sin actividad sanitaria no urgente y con aviso a los móviles por ES-Alert.
articles.body:
El Govern de la Generalitat ha suspendido este miércoles la actividad educativa —escuelas, institutos y universidades, incluida la UAB— y ha restringido la movilidad entre las siete de la mañana y las cinco de la tarde en cinco comarcas por la previsión de lluvias torrenciales, con alerta roja del Servicio Meteorológico de Cataluña, que no descarta superar los 40 litros por metro cuadrado en media hora.

Las comarcas afectadas son el Baix Llobregat, el Vallès Occidental, el Garraf y el Alt y Baix Penedès, en el entorno de Barcelona. La consellera de Interior, Núria Parlon, anunció además la suspensión de la actividad sanitaria no urgente, de los centros de día de mayores y con discapacidad y del deporte al aire libre, y pidió teletrabajar "si es posible". Protecció Civil comunicó las restricciones el martes por la tarde a través de un mensaje ES-Alert a los móviles de los vecinos.

## Tormentas 'con impacto considerable'

El periodo de mayor riesgo se espera entre las ocho y las dos de la tarde. El jefe de predicción del Meteocat, Santi Sagalà, precisó que no se trata "ni de una levantada ni de una DANA", pero Parlon advirtió de que los chubascos pueden ser "torrenciales con un impacto considerable". El aviso naranja se mantiene en el Vallès Oriental, el Ripollès, el Berguedà y el Solsonès.

Es el segundo día de curso que se pierde por el agua en menos de una semana: el episodio llega 24 horas después de que las tormentas cruzaran Tarragona con dos muertos, y tras unas noches tórridas que han complicado dormir a miles de vecinos del litoral catalán.

articles.headline: Begoña Gómez pide el sobreseimiento y su absolución en la audiencia previa al juicio
articles.subtitle: La defensa de la esposa de Sánchez y la de su asesora Cristina Álvarez, junto a la Fiscalía, reclaman cerrar el caso ante el juez Peinado; Hazte Oír pide abrir el juicio con jurado y hasta 13 años de cárcel. Peinado decidirá antes de jubilarse el día 27.
articles.body:
Begoña Gómez, esposa del presidente del Gobierno, se ha opuesto a la apertura de juicio con jurado popular por presuntos delitos de tráfico de influencias y malversación y ha pedido su absolución en la audiencia preliminar celebrada el martes por la tarde ante el juez Juan Carlos Peinado.

Su abogado, Jaime Campaner, solicitó el sobreseimiento del caso, en la línea de la defensa de Cristina Álvarez y de la Fiscalía, que nunca ha visto delito. Gómez no asistió —no es preceptivo— y la vista, que empezó pasadas las siete tras aceptar el juez retrasarla, duró unos cuarenta minutos.

## La petición de la acusación popular

Campaner esgrimió además la ineficacia del escrito de Hazte Oír, única acusación que pide el juicio oral, por presentar "graves defectos insubsanables": entiende que la acusación popular "trufó" su escrito de referencias a atestados policiales y declaraciones de instrucción, lo que en un procedimiento con jurado puede "contaminar" al tribunal. Las defensas habían pedido aplazar la vista —Campaner alegaba un señalamiento en Barcelona y Álvarez estaba de vacaciones—, sin éxito.

Hazte Oír mantuvo su petición: 13 años de cárcel para Gómez y seis para Álvarez, en su caso por presunta malversación. Con esta vista concluye la instrucción del caso por la cátedra que Gómez codirigió en la Universidad Complutense y las labores de su asistente en Moncloa; en julio, la Audiencia Provincial confirmó el juicio con jurado pero archivó los delitos de corrupción en los negocios y apropiación indebida y levantó las medidas cautelares.

El magistrado dictará el auto de apertura "en el mismo acto o dentro de los tres días siguientes", y se jubila el 27 de septiembre al cumplir 72 años.

articles.headline: Petrol bombs thrown at police as masked crowd of up to 50 sparks disorder in Derry's Waterside
articles.subtitle: The PSNI says the trouble near Knockwellan Park on Monday night was 'orchestrated' and that some of those involved were young people 'used and exploited' by adults. No officers were injured and calm was restored by 10.30pm.
articles.body:
Police came under attack with petrol bombs during disorder involving up to 50 masked people in the Waterside area of Derry on Monday night, the PSNI has said.

The trouble began around 7.30pm when a group described as a mix of older and younger people, some believed to be carrying weapons, was seen heading towards the playing fields at Knockwellan Park. When officers arrived they were attacked, and others in the crowd blocked the junction of the Trench Road and Strabane Old Road with wheelie bins and other items.

Supt Sinead McIldowney said the disorder was "absolutely disgraceful" and appeared to have been orchestrated. "Many of those involved have been described as young people. They are being used and exploited, and that is reprehensible," she said. No officers were injured, and calm was restored by around 10.30pm. An investigation is under way, with police appealing for footage.

## Bandsmen 'pushed them back'

DUP deputy mayor Niree McMorris said those involved were republican youths in the orbit of dissident republicanism who had tried to enter the loyalist Irish Street estate, only to be pushed back by members of the East Bank Protestant Boys flute band, who were at band practice nearby, and by police. "There was a band practice on, and they came out and pushed them back," she said.

She linked the disorder to recent sectarian graffiti in the area and said the Waterside was "an ideal spot for them to draw in the police or draw in young Protestants". The PSNI declined to confirm the dissident link, saying its enquiries were ongoing, and promised a heightened visible presence in the area in the coming days.

articles.headline: NI pupils' reading and maths scores fall over a decade despite strong science, PISA 2025 shows
articles.subtitle: Reading has dropped from 497 in 2015 to 482 and maths from 492 in 2018 to 473, with 30% now below the baseline level in maths, double the rate of a decade ago. Paul Givan calls the results 'a wake-up call'.
articles.body:
Northern Ireland's 15-year-olds have recorded a significant decade-long decline in reading and maths in the PISA 2025 international tests, results published on Tuesday show, although they remain comfortably above the OECD average in all three areas.

Almost 3,500 pupils from 104 schools took the computer-based tests last autumn. Reading fell from 497 in 2015 to 482, and maths from 492 in 2018 to 473. Science held up at 492 — among the best in the world, with no significant change since 2015. The worrying trend is at the bottom: 30% of pupils are now below Level 2, the international baseline for maths, compared with 19% a decade ago.

NI outperforms Wales, is similar to Scotland and trails England and the Republic in every subject. The Republic, ranked seventh globally in reading, scored 500 against NI's 482. The OECD warned of a worldwide decline in teenagers' reading skills.

## 'Relative success is not sufficient progress'

Education Minister Paul Givan called the results "a wake-up call". "We should not confuse relative success with sufficient progress," he said, pointing to his TransformED reform programme and to persistent gaps linked to disadvantage: pupils eligible for free school meals scored significantly below their peers in every domain.

Dr Graham Gault of NAHT NI said the findings showed "clear signs of pressure within the system" against a backdrop of "severe budget constraints", with schools "being asked to do more with less". The results come weeks after NI students again outperformed England and Wales in top GCSE grades.

articles.headline: Row after Army and RAF recruit at Derry jobs fair, a year on from last year's ban
articles.subtitle: The Derry Anti-War Coalition says the stands breach council policy opposing militarism, while a DUP MLA condemns 'oppressive and totalitarian behaviour' by elected representatives. The event at the Ebrington Hotel was supported by the council.
articles.body:
A row has broken out over the presence of British Army and RAF recruiters at the Cross Border Jobs Fair held on Tuesday at the Ebrington Hotel in Derry, an event promoted by Derry City and Strabane District Council.

The Derry Anti-War Coalition accused the council of acting against its own agreed positions — it formally supports the BDS campaign and opposes militarism — and said a councillor had raised objections before the event. Independent councillor Gary Donnelly confronted the recruiters, telling them the Ebrington complex should not be "a recruitment base for imperialist cannon fodder".

The Army and RAF were among more than 30 employers at the fair, which was led by the Department for Communities; the group separately claimed the Army stall was temporarily closed.

DUP Foyle MLA Julie Middleton hit back, saying the armed forces and PSNI "offer honourable and rewarding career paths" and should always be welcome at jobs fairs. "The oppressive and totalitarian behaviour of some elected representatives seeking to impose their narrow political ideology is deeply concerning," she said.

The controversy echoes last September, when the Army withdrew from the same fair at the council-owned Foyle Arena after Sinn Féin, the SDLP and independent councillors objected, prompting criticism from the DUP leader Gavin Robinson and then justice minister Naomi Long. A council spokeswoman stressed that this year's event was led by the department, which coordinates the fair with the Labour Market Partnership and the Republic's Department of Social Protection.

articles.headline: UK sanctions West Bank settlements and accuses Israel of tolerating 'ethnic cleansing'
articles.subtitle: Ed Miliband announced a new sanctions regime over illegal settlements, with France and Canada joining; Israel retaliated by closing the UK's consulate in East Jerusalem and banning 11 MPs from entering the country.
articles.body:
The UK has announced sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, with Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband telling MPs the government agrees that "there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank, perpetrated by settler terrorists".

Over the next six to nine months Britain will introduce a comprehensive sanctions regime: settlement goods will be banned, as will services supporting settlement expansion and advertising for settlements in the UK. France and Canada announced matching measures, and a joint statement with 11 other countries — including Spain and Ireland — backed trade restrictions on settlement goods.

"This marks the beginning of a new approach... which not only calls out injustice and suffering but acts," Miliband said, weeks after Israel opened tenders for some 1,200 settlement homes in the E1 area east of Jerusalem, which he said would make a two-state solution "unviable". He also said war crimes "appear to have been committed" in Gaza, referring to UN commission of inquiry findings.

## Furious Israeli response

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar called the accusation an "outrageous lie" and announced counter-measures: the UK's consulate in East Jerusalem will close, British representatives will be removed from the International Gaza Support Center, and 11 UK MPs — including Jeremy Corbyn, Diane Abbott and the Greens — will be barred from Israel. President Isaac Herzog said the decision "will fall on the wrong side of history".

US ambassador Mike Huckabee warned of American retaliation with "huge economic impact on British businesses". Shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat accused the government of enacting policies "the Foreign Office knows won't work". Some 700,000 Jewish settlers live in about 160 settlements alongside roughly 3.3 million Palestinians, amid a surge in settler violence since the Gaza war began.

articles.headline: Trump bans Canadian alcohol, dairy and motorcycles as the trade war with Canada escalates
articles.subtitle: Import bans signed under Section 338 take effect on 29 September in response to Canada's retaliatory tariffs on $20bn of US goods. Canadian PM Mark Carney says the pivot away from the US 'will come at a cost'.
articles.body:
The United States is banning imports of Canadian alcohol, dairy products and motorcycles, Donald Trump announced on Tuesday, in a sharp escalation of the trade war between the two neighbours.

The White House said the proclamations, signed under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, respond to Canada's "discrimination" against American commerce — most provinces have kept US liquor off government-run shelves throughout the dispute. The bans take effect on 29 September, with further product changes and new 50% tariffs on other Canadian goods — from cheeses to golf carts — from 15 September. Trump also directed officials to shut Canadian products out of large US government contracts unless Ottawa restores "full and fair reciprocity".

Canada's dollar-for-dollar retaliatory tariffs on $20bn of US goods came into force at midnight, hitting steel, clothing and furniture. Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a video address that the country's pivot away from its largest trading partner "will come at a cost", but insisted Canada will not back down.

Negotiations collapsed in late August, and no new talks are scheduled. Trump had warned Canadian aircraft maker Bombardier on Monday that it must move manufacturing to the US or lose its market there. The two had been each other's closest allies: the US takes roughly two-thirds of Canada's exports, while Canada is America's second-largest trading partner after Mexico. Tensions have spilled beyond trade — last month Trump ordered Lake Ontario renamed "Lake America", to uproar in Canada.

articles.headline: Tung Chee-hwa, Hong Kong's first leader after the handover from Britain, dies aged 89
articles.subtitle: The shipping tycoon handpicked by Beijing governed the city from 1997 to 2005, through the Asian financial crisis, SARS and the half-million-strong protest against the Article 23 security bill. He resigned in March 2005.
articles.body:
Tung Chee-hwa, the shipping magnate who became Hong Kong's first chief executive after Britain handed the territory back to China in 1997, has died aged 89. His office said he passed away on Tuesday night surrounded by his family, and described him as devoted to his country and its people.

Born in Shanghai in 1937, Tung trained as a mechanical engineer at Liverpool University and worked for General Electric in the US before joining his father's Orient Overseas shipping group in Hong Kong in 1969, taking over the helm a decade later. Beijing's backing was unmistakable: at a January 1996 reception, President Jiang Zemin crossed a packed hall to shake his hand, in a famously photographed signal of support.

## A turbulent eight years

His tenure, which began when he succeeded the last British governor Chris Patten, was buffeted by the Asian financial crisis, a bird flu outbreak and the 2003 Sars epidemic. His greatest political challenge came in July 2003, when half a million people marched against his proposed national security law — the Article 23 bill — which his administration then abandoned.

Tung resigned in March 2005, officially on health grounds, though some said Beijing pressed him to go after months of public criticism. He later served as vice-chairman of China's top political advisory body and remained a loyalist voice as freedoms narrowed; Beijing imposed its own national security law on Hong Kong in 2020, which critics called "the end of Hong Kong". He had not appeared in public since July 2021, months before heart surgery.

articles.headline: Meta ran hundreds of AI-generated child sexual abuse ads, some using real children's photos, report finds
articles.subtitle: The Tech Transparency Project found 332 adverts on Facebook and Instagram, 84 of them in India — many still running after the government ordered Meta to remove such content. Lawmakers in the US and Australia have opened inquiries.
articles.body:
Meta ran hundreds of paid adverts using AI-generated child sexual abuse material over the past ten months, a report by the Washington-based Tech Transparency Project (TTP) has found — including images of real children, among them a minor member of a European royal family whose official photograph had been turned into a graphic sex video.

The report, published on Tuesday, counted 332 such adverts on Facebook and Instagram, most of them in August, and said the majority began with an innocent photo of a preteen that AI morphed into abuse as the video played. About a quarter of the ads ran in India, 78 of them after New Delhi ordered Meta to remove CSAM content following a BBC Eye investigation in July.

TTP says a dozen or more ads appeared even after it alerted the company, and that Meta's own reporting system replied to 43 of 55 flagged Indian ads that they did not violate advertising standards.

The ads directed users to AI "nudify" apps, mostly built by Chinese developers and often placed by Meta's Chinese advertising partners. Meta said it "does not tolerate nudify apps or any kind of child exploitation", that most ads had already been removed and that total ad spend was under $5,000.

Senator Mark Warner and the attorneys general of Michigan and Florida, plus Australia's eSafety regulator, say they are investigating. Activists note the findings come as Meta pays up to $16.7bn to settle lawsuits over alleged harm to children from its platforms.

articles.headline: Chrome now ships a new version every two weeks as Google responds to the AI security era
articles.subtitle: Chrome 153, out on 8 September, starts the faster cycle on desktop, Android and iOS. Google says AI-powered attacks demand smaller windows between a fix landing and reaching users. Weekly security updates continue between releases.
articles.body:
Google has switched Chrome to a two-week release cycle, halving the four-week cadence the browser has followed since 2021 — and the six-week one before that. The new rhythm begins with Chrome 153, released on Tuesday across desktop, Android and iOS, with a beta version now shipping three weeks ahead of each stable release.

The change is driven by security in the AI era. Google says automated tools and community bug reports have pushed up the volume of fixes, while faster-moving threats — some of them AI-assisted — demand a shorter window between a patch landing in the codebase and reaching users' devices. The goal is to shrink the "N-day" gap: the time a known vulnerability stays exploitable.

Weekly security updates, introduced in 2023, continue between milestones, and enterprise "Extended Stable" keeps its slower eight-week track. The Dev and Canary channels are unchanged.

There is a competitive motive too. AI-assisted software development has made it easier for new browsers to emerge and iterate, and Chrome itself is experimenting with more AI features that benefit from rapid release cycles. Mozilla, Microsoft and Brave have already begun moving to two-week schedules, following Chrome's lead.

articles.headline: Google-backed revival of an Iowa nuclear plant wins a $1.9 billion US government loan
articles.subtitle: NextEra Energy secured the Department of Energy loan to restart the Duane Arnold Energy Center, whose power Google agreed to buy for 25 years. It is the second federal loan backing an AI-era nuclear restart after Three Mile Island.
articles.body:
The owner of the Iowa nuclear plant Google wants to resurrect has secured a loan of up to $1.9 billion from the US Department of Energy to pay for it. NextEra Energy announced the financing on Tuesday for the Duane Arnold Energy Center, which shut down in 2020 after more than four decades of operation.

Google agreed last October to buy power from the 615-megawatt plant under a 25-year agreement, the deal that made the restart financially viable. NextEra says the project remains subject to licensing approval by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, and the plant is scheduled to resume operations in early 2029.

The loan is the second of its kind, a signal that the Trump administration sees revived atomic power as a key electricity source for the data centres fuelling the AI boom. Last year the department lent $1 billion to Constellation Energy to restart a reactor at Pennsylvania's Three Mile Island — the Crane Clean Energy Center — which is under contract to power Microsoft's data centres, generating 835 megawatts when it returns in 2028.

articles.headline: OpenAI claims a proof of the Navier–Stokes problem — and a row erupts over how it got there
articles.subtitle: An internal model using some 10,000 agents produced a solution to one of the Millennium Prize Problems. An NYU mathematician who solved a related problem first says OpenAI 'fought dirty', raising questions about training data and credit.
articles.body:
OpenAI says it has solved one of the hardest open problems in mathematics: the Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness question, one of seven Millennium Prize Problems carrying a $1 million bounty. In a paper and Lean-formalised proof published on Tuesday, the company describes how an unreleased internal model — "significantly more capable than GPT-6 Astra" — coordinated about 10,000 agents that exchanged 2.7 million messages and used roughly 130 billion tokens to find a resolution in about 88 hours.

The proof shows that smooth, three-dimensional fluid motion described by the equations can develop a singularity in finite time; verification with GPT-6 Astra took a further 17 hours. OpenAI will not claim the prize money, and calls the result a snapshot of how fast AI is advancing rather than a culmination.

## The row over how it happened

Before the announcement a dispute had erupted. Tristan Buckmaster, an NYU mathematics professor, had published results a day earlier on a related problem — the forced Euler equations — solved with Anthropic researcher Levent Alpöge after almost a year of work using Codex and Claude.

Buckmaster says OpenAI learned of their progress, then set an entire team on the same route, which he calls "not the direction one arrives at in a few days by giving a model the problem statement".

OpenAI denies it: it says it heard only rumours on 1 September, saw none of the pair's work, and accessed no specific user data — while conceding it "cannot rule out" that de-identified customer data improved its models. Buckmaster counters that this admits training on data from after their result.

OpenAI's Sebastian Bubeck calls the accusations "false and inflammatory", while observers note the episode mirrors computer security, where a rumour of an unpatched bug is enough to trigger a race to exploit it first.

articles.headline: ChatGPT Images 2.5 arrives with a Sketch canvas and sharper, faster image editing
articles.subtitle: OpenAI's new image model generates up to 50% faster than version 2.0, keeps faces more recognisable in reference photos and edits more precisely. A new Sketch feature lets users draw a rough idea in ChatGPT and refine it.
articles.body:
OpenAI has released ChatGPT Images 2.5, its new state-of-the-art image model, with sharper details, more natural lighting and better preservation of the people in your reference photos. The company says generation is up to 50% faster than Images 2.0, and that the model follows editing instructions more reliably across long, multi-turn conversations.

A new Sketch feature lets you draw directly in ChatGPT — a rough room layout, an outfit idea or a doodle — and use the drawing as the visual guide for a final image; just type "@Sketch".

There are also templates for popular formats such as posters and product shots, the ability to leave comments on an image to point the model at exactly what to change, and prompt sharing so others can reuse an idea with their own photos.

The update lands in ChatGPT, ChatGPT Work and Codex across desktop, mobile and web. Developers get two new API models: GPT-Image-2.5 Flare for speed and quality at half the latency of its predecessor, and GPT-Image-2.5 Sunburst for precision work with longer generation times. OpenAI notes that people now create more than three billion images a week across its image products, and stresses that C2PA metadata and invisible watermarking remain in place to identify AI-made images.

articles.headline: Meta launches Muse, a personal AI agent that does your chores — if you trust it
articles.subtitle: The agent from Meta Superintelligence Labs can send emails, book travel, negotiate bills and buy things via a single-use card. Meta is leaning on a secure virtual machine design to win over users it has burned before.
articles.body:
Meta has launched Muse, a personal AI agent that automates everyday tasks — sending emails, booking travel, turning recipe videos into shopping lists, lowering bills and even selling your car. It arrives today as an app on iOS and Android, on the web at muse.ai and inside WhatsApp, with Meta's AI glasses support promised soon. It is free to start, with paid tiers at $20 and $100 a month for heavier use.

Muse is the flagship consumer bet of Meta Superintelligence Labs, the unit Mark Zuckerberg created about a year ago to chase OpenAI and Anthropic. The company is late to the agent race — rivals include viral assistants OpenClaw and Instinct — so it is trying to differentiate on privacy and safety.

## Built to be watched

Every user's activity runs in what Meta calls a Secure VM, an isolated cloud computer where the agent works and browses the web. A separate "Sentinel" agent monitors everything trying to leave that machine, matching it against user permissions or raising a human check-in prompt — delivered directly, not through the model, to resist prompt-injection attacks.

Purchases go through Stripe's Link with a single-use card number, and Meta says Muse never sees passwords, never shares data with its ad systems, and lets users opt out of training on their data.

The launch arrives less than two weeks after Meta agreed to an $18 billion multistate settlement over harms to consumers, and analysts note the company's history with the FTC and Cambridge Analytica may weigh on adoption. A future "Confidential VM", built with Signal creator Moxie Marlinspike, would encrypt each user's agent space so that even Meta cannot read it, with external audits and a bug bounty paying up to $300,000.

articles.headline: Coding agent startup Cognition doubles its valuation to $48 billion as AI coding revenue surges
articles.subtitle: The maker of Devin raised $2 billion from Andreessen Horowitz, Accel and others, citing run-rate revenue that nearly doubled in four months to about $900 million. Nvidia joined both as investor and customer.
articles.body:
Cognition, the startup behind the AI coding agent Devin, said on Tuesday it has raised $2 billion in a Series E round at a $48 billion valuation — nearly double its $26 billion mark from May. The round was led by new investors Andreessen Horowitz and Accel, alongside existing backers Founders Fund, General Catalyst and Avenir, with a syndicate of more than 30 firms. Nvidia participated, and is also a named customer.

The valuation signals that investors believe the AI coding market can sustain several major players rather than collapsing into a winner-take-all contest, and that autonomous software engineering is becoming a real revenue business. Cognition says its annualised run-rate revenue has grown from $492 million in May to almost $900 million — roughly an 80% jump in four months — and that its own product now writes over 90% of its own code.

Analysts caution that the figure is company-stated run-rate, not audited revenue, and that the round prices sustained compounding at about 53 times that run-rate. Cognition burns heavily too: it expects to spend around $800 million this year, much of it leasing Nvidia server clusters and training its own models, undercutting its own "models are commoditised" thesis. The company's stated target is a $4–5 billion run-rate by the end of 2026.
